User Viewpoint:
In order to permit other threads to operate during cooperative multitasking, the user must specifically invoke osYield() within their thread functions. A thread monopolizes the CPU and totally starves other threads if it persists in an endless loop. The user is solely responsible for maintaining system fairness, but they also have complete control over when their thread relinquishes the processor.
Because the OS automatically interrupts threads after their timeslice expires and switches to other threads, pre-emptive multitasking allows the user to write thread functions without worrying about yielding. The OS forcibly removes threads from the CPU, so even poorly written threads that never yield cannot starve the system. The user loses fine-grained control over scheduling choices but gains automatic fairness.
OS Implementation:
The OS only needs to use the SVC mechanism to enable voluntary context switching for cooperative multitasking. The OS sets the PendSV pending bit to execute a context switch via PendSV_Handler and osSched() when osYield() initiates SVC #4. The OS does not change threads unless specifically asked to do so.
The OS must actively control thread execution time with the SysTick timer in order to perform preemptive multitasking. The OS automatically starts PendSV for an involuntary context switch when the current thread's runtime counter hits zero, which is decremented by SysTick_Handler every 1 ms. In order to preserve cooperative and preemptive scheduling at the same time, the OS also resets thread runtime values when threads yield or start. In contrast to cooperative scheduling, this necessitates timer-driven interrupt handling and extra thread metadata (timeslice, runtime).
